summary: Guidance for designers of key management protocols that work with Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting systems. It stresses that designing secure, long-lasting key management is hard, and that groups without deep expertise should not invent their own. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: This Best Current Practice gives designers a set of security requirements for AAA key management. It explains how to limit who can access keys, keep session keys fresh, and prevent one compromise from exposing unrelated keys.

subtitle: Design requirements for protocols that distribute keys through authentication, authorization, and accounting systems.

tldr.problem: AAA-based key management is difficult to design securely, and ad hoc protocols can have poorly understood security properties.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives requirements and recommendations for algorithm choice, fresh keys, limited key scope, replay protection, authentication, authorization, and key naming.
tldr.outcome: The guidance applies to documents requesting publication as IETF RFCs and is known as the Housley Criteria. It is published as BCP 132.

today: RFC 4962 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 132), published in July 2007. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: What the Guidance Covers
sections.content:
Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) key management often combines the AAA protocol with protocols for authentication and security-association setup. This RFC gives architectural guidance to designers of those systems and applies to documents seeking publication as IETF RFCs.

The authors warn that secure, long-lasting key management is difficult even for experts. The requirements mostly grew from a presentation by Russ Housley to the AAA Working Group at IETF 56; the set became known as the Housley Criteria.
sections.plainLanguage: This document gives security guidance for systems that use AAA to manage keys. Its requirements are intended to prevent common design weaknesses.

sections.title: Requirements and Compliance
sections.content:
A proposal is not compliant if it fails a MUST or MUST NOT requirement. A proposal that meets all MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, and SHOULD NOT requirements is unconditionally compliant; one that meets only the MUST-level requirements is conditionally compliant.

The guidance is mandatory to implement, but a deployment is not required to use every feature. Configuration at deployment can result in a system that does not follow every recommendation.
sections.plainLanguage: A design fails compliance if it breaks any MUST requirement. It can still be implemented when deployment settings do not use every feature.

sections.title: Why Key Management Needs Care
sections.content:
The RFC reviews flaws discovered in key-management protocols over time. It says earlier defects were obvious after publication, but experts had not identified them beforehand. It therefore calls for review by multiple experts and notes that formal methods can help uncover problems.

Algorithm independence lets a system replace a cryptographic algorithm when weaknesses appear. Least privilege limits each party to the keying material and permissions its role needs. The RFC uses the history of DES and AAA authentication mechanisms to explain why both principles matter.
sections.plainLanguage: Key-management flaws can remain hidden until someone studies them closely. Designs should allow algorithms to change and should give each participant only the keys needed for its role.

sections.title: Core Requirements for Key Protocols
sections.content:
AAA key management provides keys when a peer and authenticator cannot derive them themselves. The protocol MUST be algorithm-independent and support negotiation, with at least one mandatory-to-implement algorithm suite. Session keys MUST be strong, fresh, independent of one another, and protected for confidentiality and integrity.

AAA, EAP, and secure-association exchanges MUST have replay protection. Every party MUST be authenticated, and peer and authenticator authorization MUST be checked. A protocol SHOULD securely confirm cipher-suite selection and detect rollback attempts.
sections.plainLanguage: Each session needs a fresh key that does not expose other session keys if it is compromised. The protocol must also authenticate and authorize participants and reject replayed messages.

sections.title: Key Scope, Names, and Context
sections.content:
Parties MUST NOT have access to keying material that they do not need. A protocol that establishes session keys MUST state which parties can access each key. Every key MUST have a unique name, and that name MUST NOT reveal the keying material.

Keying material MUST be bound to its intended use, the parties allowed to access it, and its expected lifetime. A child key SHOULD NOT outlast its parent key. A compromise of one peer or authenticator MUST NOT expose keys held by other peers or authenticators; group keys are an explicit exception.
sections.plainLanguage: Each key needs a unique, non-secret name and a clear record of who may use it. Keeping key scopes separate limits the damage from a compromise.

sections.title: Recommendations and Trust Relationships
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that EAP methods provide identity confidentiality where useful. If authorization restricts a peer, such as by key lifetime or network identifier, the peer SHOULD be told about the restriction.

The AAA server is trusted to distribute only the keying material established with the peer and only to the authorized authenticator. The authenticator is trusted not to pass that material to others. Management information bases MUST NOT expose private or symmetric keys, though they MAY expose key names and context or permit key deletion.
sections.plainLanguage: Participants need a shared understanding of which identities and restrictions apply to a key. Management tools may show key names, but must not expose private or symmetric key values.
